Learner group/sample: Third-year medical students and practicing doctors; n = 18, including 15 students and 3 doctors
AI tool or intervention: AI virtual patient using LLM and natural voice synthesis
Affective-domain focus/measure: Communication, psychological safety, usability, engagement, fidelity, immersion, debriefing; ITEM-based survey and focus groups
Key findings: Students reported high intrinsic motivation, usability, psychological safety, and positive learning experience. Participants valued the safe practice environment and immediate feedback.
Table_3.docx: AI tool / intervention: AI virtual patient using LLM and natural voice synthesis
Table_3.docx: Educational context: Primary care consultation for prostate cancer risk assessment
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Fidelity and immersion were only moderate. Technical limitations and realism constraints were reported; the AI virtual patient did not yet match human standardised patient authenticity.

AI tool or intervention: DIALOGUE, GPT-4o-based AI-simulated patient with automated feedback
Affective-domain focus/measure: Diagnostic communication, empathy-related outcomes, patient-centered consultation; eight-domain communication rubric
Key findings: Mean total performance increased by 36.7 points; high-performing students increased from 0% to 70%. Gains were significant across all rubric domains.
Table_3.docx: AI tool / intervention: DIALOGUE, GPT-4o-based AI-simulated patient with automated feedback
Table_3.docx: Comparator: No parallel comparator; pre-test AI encounters and post-test human standardised patient consultations
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Single-arm design, small sample, short follow-up, and possible influence of digital self-efficacy. Long-term transfer to real clinical encounters was not established.

Learner group/sample: Senior clinical medical students; n = 82, AI-VSP n = 40 and traditional SP n = 42
AI tool or intervention: AI-based virtual standardized patients using DeepSeek-chat and SEGUE framework
Affective-domain focus/measure: Physician–patient communication, patient-centered interaction; SEGUE total, Content, and Process scores; qualitative feedback
Key findings: Both groups improved, but AI-VSP students achieved higher total and Content scores and completed more training sessions. AI-VSPs were perceived as repeatable, convenient, realistic, intelligent, and helpful.
Table_3.docx: AI tool / intervention: AI-based virtual standardised patients using DeepSeek-chat and SEGUE framework
Table_3.docx: Educational context: Physician–patient communication training after medical ethics course
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Process scores were similar between groups, and AI-VSPs did not necessarily improve empathy or relational communication.

Learner group/sample: Undergraduate medical students; n = 396 eligible, n = 378 completed at least one survey
AI tool or intervention: SimConverse web-based AI-driven voice-recognition virtual patient simulator
Affective-domain focus/measure: Consultation skills, communication confidence, satisfaction, cost
Key findings: Both AI-based and actor-based training improved self-reported communication skills. AI-CST was slightly inferior to actor-based training but substantially cheaper per student.
Table_3.docx: AI tool / intervention: SimConverse web-based AI-driven voice-recognition virtual patient simulator
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Outcomes were self-reported, satisfaction was lower for AI-CST, and the intervention was a single-session simulation rather than long-term clinical assessment.

Learner group/sample: Fourth-year medical students; AI group n = 35, historical control n = 110
AI tool or intervention: GPT-4 Turbo AI-simulated patients with feedback, delivered via miibo and LINE
Affective-domain focus/measure: Medical interview skills, confidence, OSCE preparation; pre-CC OSCE medical interview score, SBT-QA10
Key findings: The AI intervention group achieved higher medical interview OSCE scores than controls. The platform was safe and supported repeated practice.
Table_3.docx: AI tool / intervention: GPT-4 Turbo AI-simulated patients with feedback, delivered via miibo and LINE
Table_3.docx: Educational context: Medical interview practice before pre-clinical clerkship OSCE
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Non-randomised historical comparison; short-term OSCE-based assessment only; limited effect on non-verbal communication; should supplement rather than replace traditional training.

Learner group/sample: Post-graduate medical educators, resident doctors, and doctors across 19 specialties; 69 doctors. Lay representative, n = 11, contributed as evaluators/ stakeholders
Affective-domain focus/measure: Breaking bad news, sensitive communication, professionalism; Likert agreement and preference ratings
Key findings: AI-generated guidance produced highly rated statements and was preferred by 61% of respondents, compared with 22% preferring the traditional approach.
Table_3.docx: Educational context: Generic Professional Capabilities and postgraduate breaking-bad-news guidance
Table_3.docx: Comparator: Human-generated guidance from facilitated trainer–resident discussions
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Did not assess learner performance or real communication behaviour. Small numbers limited subgroup generalisability; AI content required appropriate curation.

AI tool or intervention: ChatGPT-3.5 simulated patient using SPIKES breaking-bad-news scenario
Affective-domain focus/measure: Confidence, professionalism, trust in AI, difficult communication; pre–post Likert survey and grading comparison
Key findings: Student confidence in breaking bad news increased significantly, and trust in ChatGPT for communication skills and professionalism training also increased.
Table_3.docx: AI tool / intervention: ChatGPT-3.5 simulated patient using SPIKES breaking-bad-news scenario
Table_3.docx: Comparator: No intervention comparator; ChatGPT and faculty grading compared
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Small sample; ChatGPT grading was inconsistent and differed from faculty ratings. Emotional realism, voice tone, body language, and non-verbal cues were limited.

AI tool or intervention: BRAVE generative AI-based breaking-bad-news simulator with reflective debrief and SPwICES-mapped feedback
Affective-domain focus/measure: Self-efficacy, willingness, intention to apply protocol, reflective debrief, user experience
Key findings: Self-efficacy, willingness, and intention to apply the protocol improved significantly. Students perceived BRAVE as useful, realistic, safe, and feedback-rich.
Table_3.docx: AI tool / intervention: BRAVE generative AI-based breaking-bad-news simulator with reflective debrief and SPwICES-mapped feedback
Table_3.docx: Educational context: Breaking-bad-news simulation following mandatory BBN course
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Single-arm design; outcomes were self-reported. Written modality limited non-verbal cues, and occasional recognition errors were reported.

Learner group/sample: Medical students; n = 82, including 66 second semester and 16 fourth-semester students
Affective-domain focus/measure: Communication feedback, feedforward, trustworthiness, learning acceptance, avatar perception
Key findings: AI-based avatar-mediated feedforward was rated more trustworthy and more acceptable for learning than feedback. Avatar sympathy, human-likeness, trustworthiness, and attitudes toward AI influenced acceptance.
Table_3.docx: Comparator: Feedback versus feedforward comparison within the AI-avatar condition
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Participants rated feedback on a peer’s video rather than their own performance. The study assessed acceptance, not actual learning or behavioural change.

Learner group/sample: Pediatric trainees/medical interns; n = 77, ChatGPT-assisted n = 39 and traditional n = 38
Study design: Controlled experimental study with blinded assessment
Affective-domain focus/measure: Patient communication, clinical judgement, professional conduct, clinical skills; Mini-CEX and theoretical examination
Key findings: The ChatGPT-assisted group showed better Mini-CEX performance, especially in patient communication and clinical judgement, while theoretical knowledge scores were similar.
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Single-centre short intervention; long-term retention and clinical transfer were unclear. Outcomes may be influenced by implementation context and trainee acceptance.

Learner group/sample: Undergraduate medical students from five medical schools; n = 91
AI tool or intervention: ECOSBot, GPT-4o-powered standardized patient and examiner
Affective-domain focus/measure: OSCE practice, communication, professional attitude, feedback; authenticity, correctness, relevance, ICC, CUQ
Key findings: ECOSBot showed high fidelity as a standardized patient and strong agreement with human raters for global scores. Most students found the tool useful for OSCE preparation.
Table_3.docx: AI tool / intervention: ECOSBot, GPT-4o-powered standardised patient and examiner
Table_3.docx: Educational context: Nephrology OSCE training across four clinical stations
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Communication and attitude ratings were less reliable. The study validated simulation and scoring performance rather than demonstrating educational outcome improvement.

Learner group/sample: Mixed clinical experience participants; n = 7, including medical students, residents, and attending physicians
AI tool or intervention: GPT-o1 Pro and GPT-5 Pro AI-based assessment of interview transcripts in an AI-simulated patient system
Affective-domain focus/measure: Assessment reproducibility, communication evaluation; Master Interview Rating Scale, reliability, agreement, assessment time
Key findings: AI-based assessment produced scores similar to human assessment, showed strong agreement, higher consistency, and reduced evaluation time by more than half.
Table_3.docx: AI tool / intervention: GPT-o1 Pro and GPT-5 Pro AI-based assessment of interview transcripts in an AI-simulated patient system
Table_3.docx: Educational context: Clinical interview assessment using virtual patient transcripts
Table_3.docx: Reported limitations: Very small sample; single clinical case; transcript-based assessment excluded non-verbal behaviour and other contextual aspects of communication.

AI tool or intervention: Generative AI-enhanced virtual reality patient encounter simulation
Affective-domain focus/measure: Communication, confidence, motivation, critical thinking, empathy-related learning; individual interviews
Key findings: Students reported positive learning experiences and perceived the simulation as effective for practicing patient encounters, communication, confidence, and critical thinking.
Table_3.docx: AI tool / intervention: Generative AI-enhanced virtual reality patient encounter simulation
